extracted.intended_audience: antiquarians, local historians, literary scholars, and educated readers interested in folklore and historical curiosities
extracted.subtask_description: A periodical 'Notes and Queries' style column soliciting information and providing guidance on researching antiquarian subjects (folk songs, celebrated trees, local history), including descriptive characterizations of materials and suggested research methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sacred songs (carols, hymns, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sacred songs of the Low Countries (and England) are separable into Christmas carols, Easter hymns, songs in praise of the Virgin, and songs of Christian doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories when organising or describing a corpus of early sacred songs; the author invokes Hoffmann von Fallersleben's taxonomy as a framework for comparison between national repertoires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirable qualities of old carols
rubrics_metrics.description: Carols show a child-like religious spirit; they do not merely relate the scriptural story in simple ballad form but introduce small touches from social and country life to make the story more attractive and instructive and to bring it home to the hearers' hearts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate carols by their naïveté and touching simplicity; note that such qualities may include humour or elements that appear ludicrous to modern readers. Examples and literal versions are valuable for illustrating these traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of local and social detail in folk-religious songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of little touches drawn from social and country life makes sacred songs more attractive and instructive and connects them directly with audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or editing folk-religious songs, preserve and highlight vernacular/local details (e.g., occupations, domestic scenes) because they are central to the song's communicative power and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic method for researching celebrated/historical trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Antiquarian students should collect existing historical evidence relating to celebrated trees from a great variety of quarters and apply local knowledge to identify such trees wherever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry should be thorough and careful: gather references from ancient documents and charters, consult local oral knowledge, and attempt identification in the field. The periodical's wide circulation is recommended as a vehicle to coordinate such contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use charters and diplomatic sources (e.g., Codex Diplomaticus) to locate historical tree-mentions
rubrics_metrics.description: References to celebrated trees recur frequently in early charters and related documents—these are a rich source of information for identifying ancient trees and boundary marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search works like Kemble's Codex Diplomaticus for place-boundary descriptions that name trees (e.g., 'Apple-Thorn', 'Holy Oak') and transcribe relevant passages; the page gives many illustrative citations (volume and page references) as exemplars of what to look for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of tree-names and field-names as survivals of historical trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Many field-names (e.g., Mickle Thorn coppices, Broad Oak pastures, Old Yew pieces) and district names may preserve the memory or location of celebrated trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat placenames and field-names as evidential leads; when such names persist in local topography they may indicate the former presence or continued identity of historically notable trees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework for assessing the historical role/significance of conspicuous trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous trees historically played varied roles: consecrated to superstition (Holy Oak, Frigedæges Tree), served as meeting places (Hundred Tree), or marked private property and boundaries (trees prefixed by owners' names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a tree's historical importance, consider possible roles—religious/superstitious function, administrative/assembly function, boundary/landmark function—and use documentary and toponymic evidence to support interpretation.
